div.p: When Gregor Samsa woke up one morning from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a monstrous vermin. He lay on his armour-like, hard back and, if he lifted his head a little, he could see his domed, brown belly, divided by arch-shaped stiffeners, at the height of which the blanket, ready to slide down completely, could hardly be maintained. His many legs, pitifully thin compared to his usual size, flickered helplessly before his eyes.

"What has happened to me?" he thought. It wasn't a dream. His room, a real human room, just a little too small, lay quietly between the four familiar walls. Above the table, on which an unpacked collection of cloth samples was spread out - Samsa was a traveler - hung the picture that he had recently cut out of an illustrated magazine and housed in a pretty, gilded frame. It showed a lady fitted out with a fur hat and fur boa who sat upright, raising a heavy fur muff that covered the whole of her lower arm towards the viewer.

Gregor then turned his gaze to the window, and the dull weather - you could hear raindrops hitting the window pane - made him very melancholy. "How about if I sleep a little longer and forget all the nonsense," he thought, but that was completely impossible because he was used to sleeping on his right side, but in his present state couldn't get himself into that position. No matter how hard he threw himself onto his right side, he always rocked back into the supine position. He tried it probably a hundred times, closed his eyes so as not to have to see his flailing legs, and only stopped when he began to feel a light, dull pain he had never felt before in his side.

“Oh God,” he thought, “what a strenuous job I have chosen! Day in and day out on the journey. The business excitement is much greater than in the actual business at home, and in addition I am burdened with the nuisance of traveling, the worries about train connections, the irregular, bad food, ever-changing, never lasting, never cordial human traffic. Let the devil take it all!” He felt a slight itch on the top of his stomach; He slowly pushed himself closer to the bedpost on his back so he could lift his head better; found the itchy spot, which was covered in lots of little white dots that he didn't know how to judge; and wanted to touch the spot with one leg, but immediately pulled it back because the touch gave him shivers of cold.

He slipped back into his previous position. “This early rising,” he thought, “makes you feel quite stupid. Man must have his sleep. Other travelers live like harem women. For example, when I go back to the inn in the morning to write over the orders I have received, these gentlemen only sit at breakfast. I should try that with my boss; I would fly out right now. By the way, who knows whether that wouldn't be very good for me. If I hadn't held back because of my parents, I would have quit long ago, I would have gone in front of the boss and told him my opinion from the bottom of my heart. He should have fallen off the desk! It is also a strange way to sit on the desk and talk to the employee from above, who also has to get very close because of the boss's hearing loss. Well, I haven't completely given up hope yet. Once I've got the money together to pay off his parents' debt to him - it'll probably take another five or six years - I'll definitely do it. Then the big cut is made. For now, however, I have to get up because my train leaves at five."

And he looked over at the alarm clock ticking on the box. "Heavenly Father!" he thought. It was half past six and the hands were moving forward quietly, it was even half past, it was already approaching three quarters. Shouldn't the alarm have rung? You could see from the bed that it was set correctly for four o'clock; He had certainly rung the bell too. Yes, but was it possible to sleep through this furniture-shaking ringing? Well, he hadn't slept peacefully, but probably more soundly. But what should he do now? The next train was at seven o'clock; In order to catch up with him, he would have had to hurry like crazy, and the collection wasn't packed yet, and he himself didn't feel particularly fresh or agile. And even if he caught up with the train, a thunderstorm from the boss could not be avoided, because the clerk had been waiting for the five o'clock train and had long since reported his absence. It was a creature of the boss, without spine or sense. What if he called in sick? But that would be extremely embarrassing and suspicious, because Gregor had never even been sick during his five years of service. The boss would certainly come with the health insurance doctor, would blame the parents for their lazy son and would cut off all objections by pointing to the health insurance doctor, for whom there are only completely healthy but work-shy people. And by the way, would he be completely wrong in this case? Gregor actually felt quite well, apart from a really unnecessary sleepiness after his long sleep, and was even particularly hungry.

As he was thinking about all this in the greatest haste, without being able to decide to get out of bed - the alarm clock was just striking a quarter past seven - there was a careful knock on the door at the head of his bed. "Gregor," it called - it was the mother - "it's a quarter past seven. Didn't you want to drive away?" The gentle voice! Gregor was frightened when he heard his answering voice, which was unmistakably his previous one, but which was mixed with, as if from below, an uncontrollable, painful squeak, which only left the words in their clarity at the first moment, only to destroy them in the aftermath to such an extent that you didn't know whether you had heard correctly. Gregor had wanted to answer in detail and explain everything, but in these circumstances he limited himself to saying: "Yes, yes, thank you, mother, I'm getting up." Because of the wooden door, the change in Gregor's voice was probably not noticeable outside, because his mother calmed herself down with this explanation and shuffled away. But through the little conversation, the other family members became aware that, contrary to expectations, Gregor was still at home, and his father knocked on one side door, weakly, but with his fist. “Gregor, Gregor,” he cried, “what’s wrong?” And after a little while he warned again in a deeper voice: “Gregor! Gregor!” But at the other side door the sister complained quietly: “Gregor? Are you not feeling well? Do you need something?" Gregor answered to both sides: "I'm already finished," and tried to remove anything noticeable from his voice through the most careful pronunciation and by inserting long pauses between the individual words. The father also returned to his breakfast, but the sister whispered: "Gregor, open the door, I implore you." But Gregor didn't even think about opening it, but praised the caution he had learned from traveling to lock all the doors at home during the night.

First he wanted to get up quietly and undisturbed, get dressed and, above all, have breakfast, and only then think about what else to do because, he realized, he wouldn't be able to get to a sensible end to his thoughts in bed. He remembered that he had often felt a slight pain in bed, perhaps caused by lying awkwardly, which then turned out to be purely imaginary when he got up, and he was curious to see how his current ideas would gradually dissipate. He had not the slightest doubt that the change in his voice was nothing other than the harbinger of a severe cold, an occupational disease of travelers.

Throwing off the covers was easy; All he had to do was inflate himself a little and it would fall of its own accord. But it continued to be difficult, especially because it was so incredibly wide. He would have needed arms and hands to stand up; But instead he only had many little legs that were constantly in various movements and which he could not control. If he ever wanted to bend something, the first thing he did was straighten it; and if he finally managed to do what he wanted with this leg, everyone else was now working, as if released, in the highest, painful excitement. "Just don't waste time in bed," Gregor said to himself.

At first he wanted to get out of bed with the lower part of his body, but this lower part, which he had not yet seen and of which he had no real idea, turned out to be too difficult to move; it happened so slowly; and when he finally, almost wildly, pushed himself forward with all his strength and without consideration, he had chosen the wrong direction, hit the lower bedpost violently, and the burning pain he felt taught him that the lower part of his body was perhaps the most sensitive at the moment.

So he tried to get his upper body out of bed first and carefully turned his head towards the edge of the bed. This was easily achieved, and despite its width and weight, the mass of the body slowly followed the turn of the head. But when he finally got his head out of the bed in the open air, he became afraid to move forward in this way, because if he finally let himself fall like that, a miracle would have to happen if his head wasn't injured. And he couldn't lose his senses right now at any cost; He would rather stay in bed.

But when, after the same effort, he lay there again, sighing as before, and again saw his little legs fighting against each other, perhaps even more violently, and found no way to bring peace and order into this arbitrariness, he told himself again that he couldn't possibly stay in bed and that the most sensible thing to do was to sacrifice everything if there was even the slightest hope of freeing himself from the bed. At the same time, however, he did not forget to remind himself from time to time that much better than desperate decisions was calm and calm reflection. At such moments he turned his eyes as sharply as possible to the window, but unfortunately there was little reassurance or cheerfulness to be gained from the sight of the morning mist, which obscured even the other side of the narrow street. "Already seven o'clock," he said to himself as the alarm clock chimed again, "already seven o'clock and still such a fog." And for a while he lay quietly, breathing weakly, as if perhaps he expected the real and self-evident situation to return from the complete silence.

But then he said to himself: “Before the clock strikes a quarter past seven, I must be completely out of bed. By the way, someone will come out of the shop by then to ask for me, because the shop opens before seven o'clock." And he now set about rocking his entire body completely evenly out of the bed. If he let himself fall out of bed in this way, the head he intended to raise sharply as he fell would probably remain uninjured. The back seemed hard; Nothing would happen to him if he fell on the carpet. What worried him the most was the loud noise that would be heard and which would probably cause, if not fright, at least concern behind all the doors. But that had to be dared.

When Gregor was halfway out of bed - the new method was more of a game than an effort, he only had to rock in jerks - it occurred to him how easy everything would be if someone came to his help. Two strong people - he thought of his father and the maid - would have been completely sufficient; All they had to do was slide their arms under his arched back, peel him out of bed, bend down with the burden, and then just carefully allow him to complete the swing onto the floor, where the little legs would then hopefully get a sense of purpose. Well, aside from the fact that the doors were locked, should he really have called for help? Despite his distress, he couldn't help but smile at the thought.

He had already gotten to the point where he could barely keep his balance if he rocked harder, and very soon he had to make a final decision, because it was five minutes past eight in five minutes when the doorbell rang at the apartment door. "That's someone from the shop," he said to himself and almost froze as his little legs danced even more quickly. For a moment everything remained silent. "They won't open," Gregor said to himself, caught up in some senseless hope. But then of course, as always, the maid walked firmly to the door and opened it. Gregor only had to hear the visitor's first word of greeting and he already knew who it was - the authorized signatory himself. Why was Gregor the only one condemned to serve at a company where the slightest oversight was met with the greatest suspicion? If all the employees were scoundrels, wasn't there a loyal, loyal person among them who, if he hadn't used even a few morning hours for the business, became crazy with remorse and was virtually unable to get out of bed? Was it really not enough to have an apprentice ask questions - if this questioning was necessary at all - did the chief clerk himself have to come and thereby show the entire innocent family that the investigation of this suspicious matter could only be entrusted to the head of the chief clerk? And more as a result of the excitement into which Gregor was caused by these considerations than as a result of any real decision, he swung himself out of bed with all his might. There was a loud thud, but it wasn't really a crash. The fall was weakened a little by the carpet, and the back was also more elastic than Gregor had thought, which is where the not so noticeable muffled sound came from. He just didn't hold his head carefully enough and hit it; he turned it and rubbed it against the carpet in anger and pain.

"Something fell in there," said the chief clerk in the next room on the left. Gregor tried to imagine whether something similar could happen to the authorized clerk as to what happened to him today; The possibility of this actually had to be admitted. But as if in response to this question, the chief clerk in the next room took a few specific steps and made his patent leather boots creak. From the next room on the right, the sister whispered to let Gregor know: "Gregor, the authorized representative is here." "I know," said Gregor to himself; but he didn't dare raise his voice loud enough for his sister to hear.

“Gregor,” said the father from the next room on the left, “the chief clerk has come and asked why you didn’t leave on the early train. We don't know what to say to him. By the way, he also wants to talk to you personally. So please open the door. He will be kind enough to excuse the disorder in the room." "Good morning, Mr. Samsa," the chief clerk called in a friendly manner. "He's not feeling well," said the mother to the chief clerk, while the father was still talking at the door, "he's not feeling well, believe me, Mr. Chief Clerk. How else would Gregor miss a train! The boy has nothing on his mind but business. I'm almost annoyed that he never goes out in the evenings; Now he's been in the city for eight days, but he's been home every evening. He sits at our table and quietly reads the newspaper or studies timetables. It's a distraction for him when he's busy doing fretwork. For example, he carved a small frame over the course of two or three evenings; You'll be amazed at how pretty he is; it's hanging in the room; You'll see him soon when Gregor opens. By the way, I'm happy that you're here, Mr. Chief Executive Officer; we alone wouldn't have gotten Gregor to open the door; he is so stubborn; and he's definitely not feeling well, even though he denied it in the morning." "I'll be right back," said Gregor slowly and carefully and didn't move so as not to lose a word of the conversation. “I can’t explain it any other way, madam,” said the chief clerk, “I hope it’s nothing serious. On the other hand, I have to say that we business people - as you like, unfortunately or fortunately - very often simply have to overcome a slight indisposition for business reasons." "So can the authorized representative come in to see you?" asked the impatient father and knocked on the door again. "No," said Gregor. There was an awkward silence in the next room on the left, and in the next room on the right the sister began to sob.

Why didn't the sister go to the others? She had probably just gotten out of bed and hadn't even started getting dressed yet. And why was she crying? Because he didn't get up and didn't let the authorized representative in, because he was in danger of losing his job and because then the boss would go after the parents again with the old demands? Those were probably unnecessary worries for the time being. Gregor was still here and didn't have the slightest thought about leaving his family. At the moment he was probably lying there on the carpet, and no one who knew his condition would have seriously asked him to let the chief clerk in. But because of this little rudeness, for which a suitable excuse could easily be found later, Gregor couldn't be sent away immediately. And it seemed to Gregor that it would be much more sensible to leave him alone now instead of disturbing him with crying and persuading him. But it was precisely the uncertainty that oppressed the others and excused their behavior.

“Mr. Samsa,” the chief clerk now called out with a raised voice, “what’s going on? You barricade yourself in your room, answer only with yes and no, cause your parents serious, unnecessary worries and - this is only mentioned in passing - neglect your business obligations in a way that is actually unheard of. I am speaking on behalf of your parents and your boss and am seriously asking you for an immediate, clear explanation. I am amazed, I am amazed. I thought I knew you as a calm, sensible person, and now you suddenly seem to want to parade around with strange moods. This morning the boss suggested to me a possible explanation for your omission - it concerned the debt collection that had recently been entrusted to you - but I actually almost gave my word of honor that this explanation could not be correct. But now I see your incomprehensible stubbornness and have completely lost any desire to do even the slightest bit of work for you. And your position is by no means the strongest. I originally intended to tell you all this in private, but since you're letting me waste my time here, I don't know why your parents shouldn't know it too. So your recent performance has been very unsatisfactory; While this is not the time of year to do special business, we recognize that; But there is no time of year for not doing business, Mr. Samsa, there shouldn't be.”

“But Mr. Chief Executive Officer,” cried Gregor, beside himself, forgetting everything else in his excitement, “I’ll open the door straight away. A slight feeling of unease, a dizzy attack, prevented me from getting up. I'm still lying in bed now. But now I'm completely fresh again. I'm just getting out of bed. Just a moment of patience! Things aren't going as well as I thought. But I'm fine. How this can only affect a person like that! Yesterday evening I was feeling quite well, my parents know that, or rather, I had a little premonition yesterday evening. I should have seen it. Why didn't I report it to the store! But you always think that you will get through the illness without staying at home. Mr. authorized representative! Spare my parents! There is no reason for all the accusations you are now making against me; I haven't been told a word about it either. You may not have read the last few orders I sent. By the way, I'm still taking the eight o'clock train on the journey; the few hours of rest have strengthened me. Just don't stop, Mr. Authorized Officer; I'm about to go into business myself, and would you be kind enough to say so and recommend me to the boss!'

And while Gregor said all this hastily and hardly knew what he was saying, he had easily approached the box, probably as a result of the practice he had already acquired in bed, and was now trying to use it to sit up. He actually wanted to open the door, actually let himself be seen and speak to the chief clerk; He was eager to know what the others, who now so longed for him, would say when they saw him. If they were frightened, then Gregor would no longer have any responsibility and could be calm. But if they accepted everything calmly, then he would have no reason to be upset and, if he hurried, he could actually be at the station by eight o'clock. At first he slid off the smooth box a few times, but finally he gave himself one last swing and stood upright; He no longer paid any attention to the pain in his abdomen, no matter how much it burned. Now he let himself fall against the back of a nearby chair, holding on to the edges with his little legs. But with this he also gained control over himself and fell silent because he could now listen to the authorized representative.

"Did you understand a single word?" the chief clerk asked the parents. "Surely he's not making a fool of us?" "For God's sake," cried the mother, already crying, "perhaps he's seriously ill and we're torturing him. Grete! Grete!” she then shouted. “Mother?” called the sister from the other side. They communicated through Gregor's room. »You have to go to the doctor immediately. Gregor is sick. Get to the doctor quickly. Did you hear Gregor talking now?" "That was an animal's voice," said the chief clerk, remarkably quiet compared to his mother's screaming. »Anna! "Anna!" the father shouted through the anteroom into the kitchen and clapped his hands, "get a locksmith immediately!" And then the two girls ran through the anteroom with their skirts flowing - how had the sister gotten dressed so quickly? -- and tore open the apartment door. You didn't even hear the door slam; They had probably left them open, as is usual in apartments where a great misfortune has occurred.

But Gregor had become much calmer. So you no longer understood his words, although they seemed clear enough to him, clearer than before, perhaps as a result of your ear getting used to them. But at least they now believed that there was something wrong with him and were prepared to help him. The confidence and security with which the initial arrangements had been made made him feel good. He felt included in the human circle again and hoped for great and surprising achievements from both the doctor and the locksmith, without actually distinguishing between them. In order to have as clear a voice as possible for the crucial meetings that were approaching, he coughed a little, although he tried to do so in a very muffled manner, since this noise might sound different from a human cough, which he no longer dared to decide for himself. It had now become completely quiet in the next room. Maybe the parents were sitting at the table with the chief clerk and whispering, maybe everyone was leaning against the door and listening.

Gregor slowly pushed the chair towards the door, let go of it there, threw himself against the door, held himself upright on it - the balls of his little legs had a little glue on them - and rested there for a moment from the effort. But then he started turning the key in the lock with his mouth. Unfortunately, it seemed that he didn't have any actual teeth - how was he supposed to grab the key? -- but the jaws were of course very strong, with their help he actually got the key moving and didn't pay attention to the fact that he undoubtedly caused himself some kind of damage, because a brown liquid came out of his mouth, flowed over the key and dripped onto the floor. "Just listen," said the chief clerk in the next room, "he's turning the key." That was a great encouragement for Gregor; But everyone should have shouted to him, even his father and mother: "Fresh, Gregor," they should have shouted, "always close, close to the lock!" And in the idea that everyone was watching his efforts with excitement, he dug into the key with all the strength he could muster, senseless. Depending on how the key turned, he danced around the lock, now only holding himself up with his mouth, and depending on the need, he hung on the key or then pressed it down again with the entire weight of his body. The brighter sound of the lock finally snapping back literally woke Gregor up. With a sigh of relief, he said to himself: "So I didn't need the locksmith," and put his head on the handle to open the door completely.

Since he had to open the door in this way, it was actually already quite wide open and he couldn't be seen yet. He first had to slowly turn around one door, very carefully, if he didn't want to fall flat on his back before entering the room. He was still busy with that difficult movement and didn't have time to pay attention to anything else when he heard the chief clerk utter a loud "Oh!" - it sounded like the wind was rushing - and now he saw him, who was next at the door, pressing his hand against his open mouth and slowly backing away, as if an invisible, evenly acting force was driving him away. The mother - she stood here despite the chief clerk's presence, her hair still standing up from the night - first looked at her father with folded hands, then took two steps towards Gregor and fell down in the middle of her skirts spreading out around her, her face lowered to her chest, completely invisible. The father clenched his fist with a hostile expression, as if he wanted to push Gregor back into his room, then looked uncertainly around the living room, then shaded his eyes with his hands and cried until his mighty chest shook.

Gregor didn't come into the room at all, but leaned against the bolted door from the inside, so that only half of his body was visible and above that his head, tilted to the side, was visible, with which he peered over at the others. It had become much brighter now; Clearly on the other side of the street there was a section of the endless, gray-black house opposite - it was a hospital - with its regular windows breaking through the front; The rain was still falling, but only in large, individually visible drops that were literally thrown down one by one onto the earth. There were plenty of breakfast dishes on the table because for his father, breakfast was the most important meal of the day and he spent hours reading various newspapers. Just on the opposite wall hung a photograph of Gregor from his military days, depicting him as a lieutenant, his hand on his sword, smiling carelessly, demanding respect for his demeanor and uniform. The door to the anteroom was open and, since the apartment door was also open, you could see the forecourt of the apartment and the beginning of the stairs leading down.

"Well," said Gregor, well aware that he was the only one who had kept his calm, "I'll get dressed straight away, pack up the collection and drive away. Do you, do you want to let me drive away? Well, Mr. Chief Executive Officer, you see, I'm not stubborn and I like to work; Traveling is difficult, but I couldn't live without traveling. Where are you going, Mr. Authorized Officer? To the store? Yes? Will you report everything truthfully? One may be unable to work at the moment, but then is just the right time to remember one's previous achievements and to consider that later, after the obstacle has been removed, one will certainly work more diligently and more collectedly. I am so indebted to Mr. Boss, you know that very well. On the other hand, I worry about my parents and sister. I'm in a bind, but I'll work my way out of it. But don't make it any more difficult for me than it already is. Keep in business my party! You don't love the traveler, I know. You think he makes a lot of money and lives a nice life. There is no particular reason to think through this prejudice better. But you, Mr. Authorized Officer, have a better overview of the situation than the other staff, and even, to say it with complete confidence, a better overview than the boss himself, who, in his capacity as an entrepreneur, can easily allow his judgment to be swayed to the disadvantage of an employee. They also know very well that the traveler, who is away from work almost the whole year, can easily become a victim of gossip, coincidences and groundless complaints, against which it is completely impossible for him to defend himself, since he usually finds out nothing about them and only when he has finished a trip exhausted does he feel the terrible consequences firsthand at home, the causes of which can no longer be understood. Mr. Chief Executive Officer, don’t leave without saying a word to me that shows me that you agree with me, at least to a small extent!”

But the chief clerk had already turned away at Gregor's first words, and only looked back at Gregor over his twitching shoulder with pouting lips. And during Gregor's speech he didn't stand still for a moment, but, without taking his eyes off Gregor, he moved towards the door, but very gradually, as if there was a secret ban on leaving the room. He was already in the anteroom, and after the sudden movement with which he pulled his foot out of the living room for the last time, one would have thought that he had just burned the sole of his foot. In the anteroom, however, he stretched his right hand far away towards the stairs, as if an almost unearthly salvation was waiting for him there.

Gregor realized that under no circumstances could he let the authorized representative leave in this mood if his position in the business was not to be seriously jeopardized. The parents didn't understand it all that well; Over the long years they had formed the conviction that Gregor was provided for his life in this business, and besides, they were now so busy with the current worries that they had lost all foresight. But Gregor had this foresight. The authorized representative had to be held, reassured, convinced and finally won over; The future of Gregor and his family depended on it! If only the sister had been here! She was smart; She had already cried when Gregor was still lying quietly on his back. And certainly the chief clerk, this lady friend, would have allowed himself to be guided by her; She would have closed the apartment door and talked him out of his horror in the anteroom. But the sister wasn't there, Gregor himself had to act. And without thinking about the fact that he didn't yet know his current ability to move, without also thinking about the fact that his speech had possibly, probably probably not been understood, he left the door; pushed himself through the opening; wanted to go to the chief clerk, who was already ridiculously holding on to the railing of the forecourt with both hands; But immediately, looking for something to hold on to, he fell down on his many little legs with a little cry. As soon as this happened, he felt physical well-being for the first time that morning; the little legs had solid ground beneath them; they obeyed perfectly, as he noticed to his delight; even strove to carry him wherever he wished; and he already believed that the final improvement of all suffering was imminent. But at the same moment, when he was lying on the floor opposite her, not far from his mother, rocking with restrained movement, she, who seemed so completely absorbed in herself, suddenly jumped up, her arms stretched wide, her fingers spread, shouted: "Help, for God's sake help!", tilted her head as if she wanted to see Gregor better, but, in contradiction to this, ran back senselessly; had forgotten that the table was set behind her; When she reached him, she quickly sat down on him, as if absentmindedly, and didn't seem to notice that the coffee was pouring out of the large overturned pot next to her in full flow onto the carpet.

"Mother, mother," said Gregor quietly and looked up at her. The chief clerk had completely slipped his mind for a moment; On the other hand, he couldn't help but snap his jaws several times at the sight of the coffee flowing. The mother screamed again at this, fled from the table and fell into the arms of her father, who was rushing towards her. But Gregor had no time for his parents now; the chief clerk was already on the stairs; With his chin on the railing, he looked back for the last time. Gregor made an attempt to catch up with him as safely as possible; The chief clerk must have suspected something, because he jumped over several steps and disappeared; “Huh!” but he still screamed, it resonated throughout the entire stairwell. Unfortunately, this flight of the chief clerk also seemed to completely confuse the father, who had previously been relatively composed, because instead of running after the chief clerk himself or at least not hindering Gregor in his pursuit, he grabbed the chief clerk's stick with his right hand, which he had left behind on a chair with his hat and overcoat, picked up a large newspaper from the table with his left hand and, stamping his feet, began to drive Gregor back to his room by waving the stick and the newspaper. No request from Gregor helped, no request was understood, no matter how humbly he turned his head, his father only stamped his feet harder. Over there, despite the cool weather, the mother had thrown open a window and leaned out, pressing her face into her hands far outside the window. A strong draft arose between the alley and the stairwell, the window curtains flew open, the newspapers on the table rustled, individual sheets blew across the floor. The father pushed relentlessly and made hissing noises like a wild man. Now Gregor had no practice at all in walking backwards, it was really very slow. If only Gregor had been allowed to turn around, he would have been in his room straight away, but he was afraid of making his father impatient by taking so much time around, and at any moment he was threatened with a fatal blow to the back or head from the stick in his father's hand. Finally, however, Gregor had no other choice, because he realized with horror that he didn't even know how to stay in the right direction when walking backwards; and so, with incessant anxious glances at his father, he began to turn around as quickly as possible, but in reality only very slowly. Perhaps the father noticed his good intentions, because he didn't bother him, but even directed the turning movement from a distance here and there with the tip of his stick. If only it hadn't been for that unbearable hissing of his father! Gregor completely lost his head over this. He was almost completely turned around when, always listening for this hissing, he even made a mistake and turned back a little. But when he was finally happy with his head in front of the doorway, it became apparent that his body was too wide to get through easily. Of course, in his current state, the father couldn't even think of opening the other door to create sufficient passage for Gregor. His obsession was simply that Gregor had to get to his room as quickly as possible. He would never have allowed the complicated preparations that Gregor needed to get up and perhaps get through the door in this way. Perhaps, as if there were no obstacle, he was now driving Gregor forward with particular noise; Behind Gregor it no longer sounded like the voice of just one father; Now there really wasn't any fun left, and Gregor pushed himself - come what may - into the door. One side of his body rose, he lay crooked in the doorway, one side of him was completely raw, ugly stains remained on the white door, soon he was stuck and would no longer be able to move on his own, the little legs on one side hung trembling in the air, those on the other were painfully pressed to the ground - then his father gave him a strong, truly liberating push from behind, and he flew, bleeding heavily, far into his room. The door was slammed with a stick and then it was finally quiet.

Only at dusk did Gregor wake up from his heavy, fainting sleep. He would certainly not have woken up much later without being disturbed, because he felt sufficiently rested and well-slept, but it seemed to him that a fleeting step and a careful closing of the door leading to the anteroom had woken him up. The glow of the electric tram lay pale here and there on the ceiling and on the higher parts of the furniture, but down at Gregor's it was dark. Slowly, still feeling clumsily with his feelers, which he was only now learning to appreciate, he pushed his way to the door to see what had happened there. His left side appeared to be one long, unpleasantly stretching scar, and he had to practically limp on his two rows of legs. Incidentally, a little leg had been seriously injured during the morning's events - it was almost a miracle that only one had been injured - and was dragging along lifelessly.

It was only at the door that he realized what had actually drawn him there; it had been the smell of something edible. Because there was a bowl filled with sweet milk, in which little slices of white bread were floating. He almost laughed with joy because he was even hungrier than he had been in the morning, and he immediately plunged his head into the milk almost up to his eyes. But soon he withdrew it in disappointment; Not only did he find it difficult to eat because of his delicate left side - and he could only eat when his whole body cooperated, panting - but he also didn't like the milk, which was otherwise his favorite drink and which his sister had probably brought for him because of that, and he turned away from the bowl almost with reluctance and crawled back to the middle of the room.

As Gregor saw through the crack in the door, the gas had been lit in the living room, but while at this time of day the father used to read his afternoon newspaper to his mother and sometimes to his sister in a raised voice, now there was no sound. Now perhaps this reading aloud, which his sister always told him and wrote to him, had recently become out of practice. But it was also so quiet all around, even though the apartment was certainly not empty. "What a quiet life the family led," Gregor said to himself and, as he stared into the darkness ahead of him, felt great pride that he had been able to provide his parents and sister with such a life in such a beautiful apartment. But what if all peace, all prosperity, all contentment should now come to an end in terror? In order not to lose himself in such thoughts, Gregor started moving and crawled up and down in the room.

Once during the long evening one side door and once the other were opened to a small crack and quickly closed again; Someone probably felt the need to come in, but also had too many concerns. Gregor now stopped immediately at the living room door, determined to somehow bring the hesitant visitor in or at least to find out who it was; but now the door was no longer opened and Gregor waited in vain. Early on, when the doors were locked, everyone wanted to come in to him, but now that he had opened one door and the others had apparently been opened during the day, no one came anymore, and the keys were now also on the outside.

It was late at night that the light in the living room was turned off and it was now easy to see that the parents and sister had stayed awake for so long, because as you could clearly hear, all three of them were now tiptoeing away. Now no one would come in to see Gregor again until morning; So he had a long time to think undisturbed about how he should now rearrange his life. But the high, empty room in which he was forced to lie flat on the floor frightened him, without him being able to find out the cause, for it was the room he had lived in for five years - and with a half-unconscious turn and not without a slight shame he hurried under the sofa, where, despite his back being pressed a little and despite the fact that he could no longer raise his head, he immediately felt very comfortable and only regretted that his body was too wide to be completely under it to be accommodated on a sofa.

He stayed there the whole night, which he spent partly in a half-sleep, from which hunger kept waking him, and partly in worries and vague hopes, all of which led to the conclusion that he had to keep quiet for the time being and, through patience and the greatest consideration, make the family bear the inconvenience that he was forced to cause them in his current state.

Already early in the morning, it was almost night, Gregor had the opportunity to test the strength of the decisions he had just made, because the sister, almost fully dressed, opened the door from the anteroom and looked in with excitement. She didn't find him right away, but when she noticed him under the sofa - God, he had to be somewhere, he couldn't have flown away - she was so frightened that, without being able to control herself, she slammed the door shut again from the outside. But as if she regretted her behavior, she immediately opened the door again and stepped in on tiptoe, as if she were with a seriously ill person or even with a stranger. Gregor had pushed his head almost to the edge of the sofa and was watching her. Would she notice that he had left the milk, and not because he was hungry, and would she bring in another dish that would suit him better? If she didn't do it of her own accord, he would rather starve than draw her attention to it, even though he actually had a tremendous urge to rush under the sofa, throw himself at his sister's feet and ask her for something good to eat. But the sister immediately noticed with astonishment that the bowl was still full, from which only a little milk had spilled all around. She immediately picked it up, not with her bare hands, but with a scrap, and carried it out. Gregor was extremely curious about what would replace it and he thought about it in a variety of ways. But he could never have guessed what the sister really did in her kindness. To test his taste, she brought him a whole selection, all spread out on an old newspaper. There were old, half-rotten vegetables; bones from dinner surrounded by solidified white sauce; a few raisins and almonds; a cheese that Gregor had declared inedible two days ago; a dry bread, a buttered bread and a buttered and salted bread. She also put the bowl, probably intended for Gregor once and for all, into which she had poured water. And out of delicacy, since she knew that Gregor would not eat in front of her, she quickly moved away and even turned the key so that only Gregor could notice that he could make himself as comfortable as he wanted. Gregor's little legs were buzzing when it was time to eat. By the way, his wounds must have already healed completely, he no longer felt any hindrance, he was amazed at this and thought about how he had cut his finger very slightly with the knife more than a month ago, and how this wound had hurt him enough just the day before yesterday. “Should I be less sensitive now?” he thought, already sucking greedily on the cheese that he had immediately and emphatically been drawn to above all other foods. In quick succession, his eyes watering with satisfaction, he ate the cheese, vegetables and sauce; The fresh food, on the other hand, didn't taste good to him, he couldn't even stand the smell of it and even dragged the things he wanted to eat a little further away. He had long since finished everything and was just lying lazily in the same place when the nurse slowly turned the key as a signal for him to withdraw. This immediately startled him, even though he was almost asleep, and he hurried back under the sofa. But it took a lot of effort for him to stay under the sofa for even the short time that his sister was in the room, because his body had become a little rounded from the copious amounts of food and he could hardly breathe in the confines. With small attacks of suffocation, he watched with slightly bulging eyes as the unsuspecting sister used a broom to sweep up not only the leftovers, but even the food that Gregor hadn't touched at all, as if these too were no longer of any use, and how she hastily poured everything into a bucket, which she closed with a wooden lid, whereupon she carried everything out. As soon as she turned around, Gregor pulled himself out from under the sofa and stretched and puffed up.

In this way, Gregor got his food every day, once in the morning when the parents and the maid were still asleep, the second time after the general lunch, because then the parents also slept for a while, and the maid was sent away by her sister on some errand. They certainly didn't want Gregor to starve either, but perhaps they couldn't bear to find out more about his food than through hearsay; perhaps the sister also wanted to spare them what might have been only a small amount of grief, because they were actually suffering enough.

Gregor couldn't even find out what excuses had been used to get the doctor and the locksmith out of the apartment that first morning, because since he wasn't understood, no one, not even the sister, thought that he could understand the others, and so when the sister was in his room, he had to be content with just hearing her sighs and calls from the saints here and there. Only later, when she had gotten used to everything a little - of course it could never be said that she was completely used to it - did Gregor sometimes catch a remark that was meant to be friendly or could be interpreted as such. "He enjoyed it today," she said when Gregor had tidied up the food thoroughly, while in the opposite case, which gradually became more and more frequent, she would say almost sadly: "Now everything has stopped again."

But while Gregor couldn't find out any news immediately, he listened to a lot of things coming from the next room, and whenever he heard voices, he ran straight to the door in question and pressed himself against it with his whole body. Especially in the early days, there was no conversation that wasn't about him in some way, even if only in secret. For two days there were discussions at every meal about how to behave now; But people also talked about the same topic between meals, because there were always at least two family members at home, since no one wanted to stay at home alone and you couldn't leave the apartment completely under any circumstances. Also, on the very first day - it was not entirely clear what and how much she knew about what had happened - the maid kneeled and asked her mother to dismiss her immediately, and when she said goodbye a quarter of an hour later, she tearfully thanked her for the dismissal, as for the greatest benefit that had been shown to her here, and, without being asked to do so, made a terrible vow not to tell anyone the slightest thing.

Now the sister also had to cook alongside her mother; However, it wasn't much trouble because you ate almost nothing. Again and again Gregor heard how one person asked the other to eat in vain and received no answer other than: "Thanks, I've had enough" or something similar. Maybe there was no drinking. The sister often asked the father if he wanted beer and she warmly offered to get it herself, and when the father remained silent, she said, to allay his concerns, that she could also send the caretaker to get it, but then the father finally said a big "no" and nothing was said about it anymore.

During the first day, the father explained all the financial circumstances and prospects of both the mother and the sister. Every now and then he got up from the table and took out some receipt or some reserve book from his small safe deposit box, which he had saved from the collapse of his business five years ago. You could hear him unlocking the complicated lock and locking it again after taking out what he was looking for. These explanations from his father were partly the first pleasant thing Gregor had heard since his imprisonment. He had been of the opinion that the father hadn't had anything to do with the deal, at least his father hadn't told him otherwise, and Gregor hadn't asked him about it either. Gregor's only concern at the time was to do everything he could to make the family forget as quickly as possible the business misfortune that had left everyone completely hopeless. And so he had started working with a very special passion and had almost overnight turned from a small clerk into a traveling salesman who of course had completely different ways of earning money, and whose work successes were immediately transformed into cash in the form of commission, which could be placed on the table at home for the astonished and happy family. They had been good times, and they had never been repeated, at least in this splendor, even though Gregor later earned so much money that he was able and did bear the expenses of the entire family. People had just gotten used to it, both the family and Gregor, they accepted the money gratefully, he was happy to hand it over, but there was no longer any special warmth. Only his sister had still remained close to Gregor, and it was his secret plan to send her, who, unlike Gregor, loved music very much and knew how to play the violin touchingly, to the conservatory next year, regardless of the great costs that this would have to incur and that would be incurred in other ways. During Gregor's short stays in the city, the conservatory was often mentioned in conversations with his sister, but always only as a beautiful dream that was out of the question to come true, and his parents didn't even like to hear these innocent mentions; but Gregor thought of it very definitely and intended to declare it solemnly on Christmas Eve.

Such thoughts, completely useless in his current state, ran through his head as he stood there, stuck to the door, listening. Sometimes he could no longer listen due to general tiredness and let his head hit the door carelessly, but he immediately held it again, because even the small noise he had made was heard next door and had silenced everyone. "What's he doing again?" said the father after a while, apparently turning towards the door, and only then did the interrupted conversation gradually resume.

Gregor now learned quite well - because his father often repeated himself in his explanations, partly because he himself had not dealt with these things for a long time, and partly because his mother did not understand everything the first time - that despite all the misfortune, there was still a very small fortune from the old days, which the untouched interest had allowed to grow a little in the meantime. In addition, the money that Gregor had brought home every month - he had only kept a few guilders for himself - had not been completely used up and had accumulated into a small capital. Gregor, behind his door, nodded eagerly, pleased by this unexpected caution and thrift. Actually, he could have used these surplus funds to further pay off his father's debt to the boss, and the day when he could have gotten rid of this position would have been much closer, but now things were undoubtedly better the way his father had arranged it.

But this money was not at all enough to allow the family to live on the interest; It was perhaps enough to sustain the family for a year or two at the most, but it was nothing more. So it was just a sum that wasn't really allowed to be used and that had to be put aside in case of an emergency; But you had to earn the money to live on. Now the father was a healthy but old man who hadn't worked for five years and in any case didn't have much confidence in himself; He had put on a lot of fat during these five years, which were the first holidays of his arduous but unsuccessful life, and as a result had become quite clumsy. And maybe the old mother should now earn money, who suffered from asthma, who found walking around the apartment tiring, and who spent every other day on the sofa by the open window with difficulty breathing? And the sister was supposed to earn money, who was still a child at the age of seventeen and who was so fond of her previous way of life, which had consisted of dressing nicely, sleeping late, helping out in the house, taking part in a few modest amusements and, above all, playing the violin? Whenever the topic of the need to earn money came up, Gregor was always the first to let go of the door and throw himself onto the cool leather sofa next to the door, because he was very hot with embarrassment and sadness.

He often lay there all long nights, not sleeping for a moment and just pawing at the leather for hours. Or he went to great lengths to push an armchair to the window, then crawled up the window sill and, propped up in the armchair, leaned against the window, apparently only remembering the liberation that had previously been found in looking out the window. In fact, from day to day he saw things that were even a little distant more and more indistinctly; He no longer saw the hospital opposite, the sight of which he had once cursed all too often, and if he had not known that he lived on the quiet but completely urban Charlottenstrasse, he would have thought that he was looking out of his window into a wasteland in which the gray sky and the gray earth merged indistinguishably. The attentive sister had only had to see twice that the armchair was by the window, as each time after she had tidied up the room she pushed the armchair right towards the window again, and from then on even left the inner window sash open.

If Gregor had only been able to talk to his sister and thank her for everything she had to do for him, he would have endured her services more easily; But as it was, he suffered from it. Of course, the sister tried to cover up the embarrassment of the whole thing as much as possible, and the longer time passed, the better she succeeded, but Gregor also saw everything much more clearly over time. Her entry was already terrible for him. As soon as she had entered, she ran straight to the window, without taking the time to close the door, as much as she was otherwise careful to spare everyone from seeing Gregor's room, and, as if she was almost suffocating, she tore it open with hasty hands and, even though it was so cold, stayed by the window for a while and breathed deeply. She frightened Gregor twice a day with this running and noise; The whole time he was shivering under the sofa and yet he knew very well that she would certainly have been happy to spare him from it if only she had been able to stay in a room where Gregor was with the window closed.

Once, it had probably already been a month since Gregor's transformation, and there was no longer any particular reason for the sister to be astonished by Gregor's appearance, she came a little earlier than usual and found Gregor looking out of the window, immobile and in a position to be frightening. It would not have been unexpected for Gregor if she had not entered, since his position prevented her from opening the window immediately, but not only did she not enter, she even backed up and closed the door; A stranger could have thought that Gregor had ambushed her and wanted to bite her. Gregor, of course, immediately hid under the sofa, but he had to wait until midday before his sister came back, and she seemed much more restless than usual. He realized from this that the sight of him was still unbearable to her and would continue to be unbearable to her, and that she had to force herself not to run away from the sight of even the small part of his body that protruded from under the sofa. In order to spare her this sight, one day he carried the linen on his back - it took him four hours to do this work - on the sofa and arranged it in such a way that he was now completely covered and so that his sister, even if she bent over, could not see him. If in her opinion this linen had not been necessary, then she could have removed it, because it was clear enough that it could not be part of Gregor's pleasure to close himself off so completely, but she left the linen as it was, and Gregor even thought he had caught a grateful look when he carefully lifted the linen a little with his head to see how his sister was taking in the new furnishings.

During the first fortnight his parents could not bring themselves to come in to see him, and he often heard them fully acknowledging his sister's current work, whereas before they had often been annoyed with her sister because she had seemed to them to be a somewhat useless girl. But now both father and mother often waited outside Gregor's room while his sister cleaned up, and as soon as she came out, she had to tell me exactly what it looked like in the room, what Gregor had eaten, how he had behaved this time, and whether there was perhaps a slight improvement to be noticed. Incidentally, the mother wanted to visit Gregor relatively soon, but the father and sister initially held her back on grounds of reason, which Gregor listened to very carefully and which he completely approved. But later they had to hold her back by force, and when she shouted: "Let me see Gregor, he's my unfortunate son!" Don't you understand that I have to go to him?" Then Gregor thought that maybe it would be good if his mother came in, not every day of course, but maybe once a week; She understood everything much better than her sister, who, despite all her courage, was only a child and had ultimately perhaps only taken on such a difficult task out of childish carelessness.

Gregor's wish to see his mother soon came true. During the day Gregor didn't want to show himself at the window out of consideration for his parents, but he couldn't crawl much on the few square meters of floor. He found it difficult to lie still during the night, eating soon no longer gave him the slightest pleasure, and so to distract himself he took up the habit of crawling all over the walls and ceiling. He particularly liked hanging up on the ceiling; it was very different from lying on the floor; you breathed more freely; A slight vibration went through his body, and in the almost happy distraction in which Gregor found himself up there, it happened that, to his own surprise, he let go and hit the ground. But now, of course, he had completely different control over his body than before and didn't damage himself even in such a big fall. The sister immediately noticed the new entertainment that Gregor had found for himself - he also left traces of his glue here and there when he crawled - and then she decided to make it possible for Gregor to crawl to the greatest extent possible and to get rid of the furniture that prevented it, especially the chest and the desk. But now she was unable to do this alone; She didn't dare ask her father for help; The maid certainly wouldn't have helped her, because this girl, about sixteen years old, had held out bravely since her previous cook was fired, but had asked for the privilege of keeping the kitchen locked at all times and only having to open it on special call; So the sister had no choice but to go and get her mother in her father's absence. The mother also came up with exclamations of excited joy, but fell silent at the door in front of Gregor's room. First, of course, the nurse checked whether everything in the room was OK; Only then did her mother let her enter. Gregor had hurriedly folded the linen deeper and further into folds; the whole thing really just looked like a linen that had been randomly thrown over the sofa. This time too, Gregor refrained from spying under the sheet; He decided not to see his mother this time and was just glad that she had come after all. "Come on, you can't see him," said the sister, obviously leading her mother by the hand. Gregor now heard how the two weak women moved the heavy old box from its place, and how his sister kept taking on most of the work for herself, without listening to the warnings from her mother, who was afraid that she would overexert herself. It took a very long time. After a quarter of an hour of work, the mother said that it would be better to leave the box here because, firstly, it was too heavy, they wouldn't be able to finish it before the father arrived and would block Gregor's path with the box in the middle of the room, and secondly, it wasn't at all certain that removing the furniture would do Gregor any favors. To her it seems the opposite is the case; The sight of the empty wall almost depresses her heart; and why shouldn't Gregor also have this feeling, since he has long been used to the room furniture and will therefore feel abandoned in the empty room. "And isn't it the case," concluded the mother very quietly, almost in a whisper, as if she wanted to avoid Gregor, whose exact whereabouts she didn't know, even hearing the sound of the voice, because she was convinced that he didn't understand the words, "and isn't it as if we were showing by removing the furniture that we were giving up all hope of improvement and recklessly leaving him to his own devices? I think it would be best if we tried to keep the room in exactly the same condition as it was before, so that when Gregor comes back to us, he will find everything unchanged and can all the more easily forget the interim.'

As he listened to his mother's words, Gregor realized that the lack of any direct human contact, combined with the monotonous life in the midst of the family, must have baffled his mind over the course of these two months, because he could not otherwise explain why he had seriously asked for his room to be emptied. Did he really want to have the warm room, comfortably furnished with inherited furniture, transformed into a cave in which he would then be able to crawl undisturbed in all directions, but at the same time, at the same time, quickly and completely forgetting his human past? He was already close to forgetting, and only his mother's voice, which he hadn't heard for a long time, had shaken him up. Nothing had to be removed, everything had to stay, he couldn't do without the positive effects of the furniture on his condition; and if the furniture prevented him from doing his senseless crawling around, it was not a harm but a great advantage.

But unfortunately the sister had a different opinion; She had gotten into the habit, although not entirely without justification, of acting as a particularly expert to her parents when discussing Gregor's affairs, and so now her mother's advice was reason enough for her sister to insist on the removal not only of the chest and the desk, which she had initially thought of alone, but also on the removal of all the furniture, with the exception of the indispensable sofa. Of course, it wasn't just childish defiance and the self-confidence that she had recently acquired so unexpectedly and with difficulty that made her make this demand; She had actually observed that Gregor needed a lot of space to crawl, but as far as one could see, he didn't use the furniture in the slightest. But perhaps the enthusiastic spirit of girls her age, which seeks satisfaction at every opportunity, also played a role, and through which Grete was now tempted to want to make Gregor's situation even more frightening so that she could then do even more for him than she had up to now. Because in a room where Gregor alone dominated the empty walls, no one other than Grete would ever dare to enter.

And so she didn't let her mother dissuade her from her decision, who also seemed unsure in this room because of the restlessness, soon fell silent and helped her sister as best she could to get the box out. Well, Gregor could still do without the box in an emergency, but the desk had to stay. And the women had barely left the room with the box they were clinging to, groaning, when Gregor poked his head out from under the sofa to see how he could intervene carefully and as considerately as possible. But unfortunately it was the mother who returned first, while Grete was in the next room holding the box and swinging it back and forth alone, without of course moving it from its place. But the mother was not used to the sight of Gregor, he could have made her sick, and so Gregor, frightened, hurried backwards to the other end of the sofa, but could no longer prevent the sheet from moving a little at the front. That was enough to get the mother's attention. She paused, stood still for a moment and then went back to Grete.

Even though Gregor kept telling himself that nothing out of the ordinary was happening, just a few pieces of furniture were being rearranged, he soon had to admit to himself that the women's walking back and forth, their little shouts, the scratching of the furniture on the floor, had the effect on him of a great hustle and bustle that was being fed from all sides, and no matter how hard he pulled his head and legs against himself and pressed his body to the floor, he inevitably had to say to himself that he couldn't stand it all for long will. They cleared out his room; took away everything he held dear; They had already carried out the box in which the fretsaw and other tools lay; now loosened the desk that had already been firmly buried in the ground, at which he had written his assignments as a business graduate, as a middle school student, and even as a primary school student, - he really no longer had time to examine the good intentions that the two women had, whose existence he had almost forgotten, because they were already working in silence due to exhaustion, and all that could be heard was the heavy tapping of their feet.

And so he burst out - the women were leaning against the desk in the next room to catch their breath - changed the direction of his run four times, he really didn't know what to save first, then he saw the picture of the lady dressed in nothing but fur hanging on the otherwise empty wall, hurriedly crawled up and pressed himself against the glass, which held him in place and comforted his hot stomach. At least this picture, which Gregor now completely covered, would certainly not be taken away by anyone. He turned his head toward the living room door to watch the women return.

They hadn't allowed themselves much rest and were coming back; Grete had her arm around her mother and was almost carrying her. “So what do we do now?” said Grete and looked around. Then her eyes crossed with Gregor’s on the wall. It was probably only because of her mother's presence that she kept her composure, leaned her face towards her mother to stop her from looking around, and said, albeit tremblingly and without thinking: "Come on, wouldn't we rather go back to the living room for a moment?" Grete's intention was clear to Gregor; she wanted to get her mother to safety and then chase him down from the wall. Well, at least she could try! He sat on his picture and didn't give it away. He would rather jump in Grete's face.

But Grete's words had really alarmed her mother. She stepped aside, saw the huge brown spot on the flowered wallpaper, and before she actually realized that what she was seeing was Gregor, she shouted in a screaming, hoarse voice: "Oh God, oh God!" and fell over the sofa with her arms outstretched, as if she were giving up everything, and didn't move. “You, Gregor!” the sister shouted with a raised fist and an urgent look. They were the first words she had spoken directly to him since the transformation. She ran into the next room to get some essence with which she could wake her mother from her unconsciousness; Gregor also wanted to help -- there was still time to save the picture --; but he stuck firmly to the glass and had to force himself away; He then ran into the next room as if he could give his sister some advice, as he had done in the past; but then had to stand idly behind her; While she was rummaging through various bottles, she was still startled when she turned around; a bottle fell on the floor and broke; A splinter hurt Gregor's face, some caustic medicine flowed around him; Grete, without pausing any longer, took as many bottles as she could hold and ran with them to her mother; She slammed the door with her foot. Gregor was now separated from his mother, who was perhaps close to death because of his fault; He wasn't allowed to open the door if he didn't want to drive away his sister, who had to stay with her mother; he had nothing to do now but wait; and, oppressed by self-reproach and anxiety, he began to crawl, crawled over everything, walls, furniture and ceiling, and finally, in his desperation, when the whole room began to revolve around him, he fell in the middle of the big table.

A little while passed, Gregor lay there weakly, it was quiet all around, maybe that was a good sign. Then the bell rang. The girl was of course locked in her kitchen and Grete had to go open it. The father had come. "What happened?" were his first words; Grete's appearance had probably told him everything. Grete answered in a dull voice, apparently pressing her face into her father's chest: "The mother was unconscious, but she's feeling better. Gregor broke out." "I expected it," said the father, "I always told you, but you women don't want to listen." It was clear to Gregor that the father had misinterpreted Grete's all-too-brief message and assumed that Gregor had been guilty of some kind of violence. That's why Gregor now had to try to appease his father, because he had neither the time nor the opportunity to enlighten him. And so he fled to the door of his room and pressed himself against it so that his father could see straight away when he entered from the anteroom that Gregor had the best intentions of returning to his room immediately and that there was no need to drive him back, but that all one had to do was open the door and he would disappear in a moment.

But the father was in no mood to notice such subtleties. "Ah!" he cried as soon as he entered, in a tone as if he were angry and happy at the same time. Gregor pulled his head back from the door and raised it towards his father. He really hadn't imagined his father as he stood there now; However, recently, due to his new crawling around, he had neglected to pay attention to what was going on in the rest of the apartment as he had done before, and should actually have been prepared to find changed circumstances. Still, still, was that still the father? The same man who lay tired in bed when Gregor had previously gone on a business trip; who had received him in an armchair in his dressing gown on the evenings of his return home; was not really able to stand up at all, but only raised his arms as a sign of joy, and who, during the rare walks together on a few Sundays a year and on the most important holidays between Gregor and his mother, which already walked slowly in and of themselves, was still a little slower, wrapped up in his old coat, worked his way forward with his cane always carefully placed in place and, when he wanted to say something, almost always stood still and gathered his companions around him? But now he was well erect; dressed in a tight blue uniform with gold buttons, like those worn by bank servants; His strong double chin developed above the high, stiff collar of his coat; The look of the black eyes appeared fresh and attentive from under the bushy eyebrows; her otherwise disheveled white hair was combed down into a meticulous, bright parting. He threw his cap, which had a gold monogram, probably that of a bench, across the room onto the sofa and, with the ends of his long uniform coat folded back, his hands in his trouser pockets, walked towards Gregor with a grim face. He probably didn't know what he was doing; After all, he lifted his feet unusually high, and Gregor was amazed at the giant size of his boot soles. But he didn't stop there, he knew from the first day of his new life that his father only saw the greatest severity as appropriate towards him. And so he ran ahead of his father, faltering when his father stopped and then rushing forward again when his father just moved. So they made the rounds around the room several times without anything decisive happening, indeed without the whole thing having the appearance of being pursued due to its slow pace. That's why Gregor stayed on the floor for the time being, especially since he was afraid that his father might think that fleeing to the walls or ceiling was particularly evil. However, Gregor had to tell himself that he wouldn't be able to stand this running for long, because while his father took a step, he had to make countless movements. Shortness of breath was already becoming noticeable, as he had not had particularly trustworthy lungs in his earlier days. As he staggered along to gather all his strength for the run, barely keeping his eyes open; In his dullness he didn't even think of any other way to save himself than by running; and had almost forgotten that the walls were free to him, although they were blocked up with carefully carved furniture full of spikes and spikes - something flew down just next to him, slightly thrown, and rolled in front of him. It was an apple; Immediately a second one flew after him; Gregor stopped in horror; It was useless to keep running because his father had decided to bomb him. He had filled his pockets from the fruit bowl on the sideboard and was now throwing apple after apple without aiming sharply. These little red apples rolled around on the ground as if electrified, bumping into each other. A weakly thrown apple grazed Gregor's back but slid off harmlessly. However, one that immediately flew after him literally penetrated Gregor's back; Gregor wanted to drag himself along, as if the unexpected, incredible pain would go away with the change of location; but he felt as if he were pinned down and stretched in complete confusion of all senses. Only with the last glance did he see how the door of his room was thrown open and his mother rushed out in front of his screaming sister, in her shirt, because her sister had undressed her in order to give her room to breathe in her unconsciousness, how the mother then ran towards her father and on the way her untied skirts slipped one by one to the floor, and how she stumbled over her skirts and rushed into her father and hugged him, in complete union with him - well but Gregor's eyesight was already failing - the hands on the back of his father's head asked for Gregor's life to be spared.

Gregor's severe wound, from which he suffered for over a month - the apple remained in the flesh as a visible souvenir since no one dared to remove it - seemed to have reminded even his father that, despite his current sad and disgusting appearance, Gregor was a member of the family who could not be treated like an enemy, but towards whom it was the commandment of family duty to swallow the reluctance and to tolerate it, to tolerate nothing.

And even though Gregor had probably lost his mobility forever due to his wound and temporarily needed long, long minutes to cross his room like an old invalid - crawling at heights was out of the question - he received, in his opinion, a completely sufficient compensation for this aggravation of his condition in that always towards the evening the living room door, which he used to keep a close eye on one or two hours beforehand, was opened, so that he was lying in the darkness of his room, invisible from the living room. was able to see the whole family at the illuminated table and listen to their speeches, with general permission, so to speak, which was completely different from before.

Of course, it was no longer the lively conversations of earlier times that Gregor had always thought about with some longing in the small hotel rooms when he was tired and had to throw himself into the damp bedclothes. It was mostly very quiet now. The father fell asleep in his armchair soon after dinner; the mother and sister urged each other to be quiet; her mother, leaning far above the light, was sewing fine linen for a fashion store; The sister, who had taken a job as a saleswoman, learned shorthand and French in the evenings so that she might get a better job later. Sometimes the father would wake up and, as if he didn't even know that he had been asleep, he would say to his mother: "How long you've been sewing again today!" and immediately fall asleep again, while mother and sister smiled tiredly at each other.

With a kind of stubbornness, the father refused to take off his servant's uniform at home; and while the dressing gown hung uselessly on the coat hook, the father slept in his place, fully dressed, as if he was always ready to serve and was waiting for the superior's voice. As a result, the uniform, which was not new at the outset, lost its cleanliness despite all the care taken by his mother and sister, and Gregor often spent entire evenings looking at this stained dress, shining with its always-cleaned gold buttons, in which the old man slept extremely uncomfortable and yet peacefully.

As soon as the clock struck ten, the mother tried to wake up the father with quiet encouragement and then persuade him to go to bed, because it wasn't a real sleep here and the father, who had to start work at six o'clock, desperately needed it. But in the stubbornness that had gripped him ever since he became a servant, he always insisted on staying longer at the table, even though he regularly fell asleep, and, moreover, it was only with the greatest difficulty that he could be persuaded to exchange the armchair for the bed. No matter how hard his mother and sister gave him with little admonitions, he slowly shook his head for fifteen minutes, kept his eyes closed and didn't get up. His mother tugged at his sleeve, said flattering words in his ear, his sister left her task to help his mother, but his father didn't care. He just sank deeper into his chair. It wasn't until the women grabbed him under the armpits that he opened his eyes, looked alternately at his mother and his sister and used to say: "That's a life. This is the peace of my old days." And leaning on the two women, he stood up, awkwardly, as if he were the greatest burden on himself, let the women lead him to the door, waved them off and then went on independently, while his mother quickly threw down her sewing kit and his sister her pen in order to run behind his father and continue to help him.

Who in this busy and tired family had time to look after Gregor more than was absolutely necessary? The budget became more and more restricted; the maid was now released after all; a huge, bony female servant with white hair flowing around her head came morning and evening to do the hardest work; The mother took care of everything else in addition to her many sewing jobs. It even happened that various pieces of family jewelry, which the mother and sister had previously happily worn at entertainments and celebrations, were sold, as Gregor learned that evening from the general discussion of the prices achieved. But the biggest complaint was always that it was impossible to leave this apartment, which was too large for the current circumstances, because it was impossible to imagine how Gregor would be moved. But Gregor clearly saw that it wasn't just consideration for him that prevented him from moving, since he could have easily been transported in a suitable box with a few air holes; What mainly prevented the family from moving was the complete hopelessness and the thought that they had been hit with a misfortune unlike anyone else in their entire circle of relatives and acquaintances. What the world demands of poor people they fulfilled to the utmost: the father fetched breakfast for the little bank clerks, the mother sacrificed herself to do strangers' laundry, the sister ran back and forth behind the desk at the orders of the customers, but the family's strength didn't stretch any further than that.
