And the wound in Gregor's back began to hurt like new when his mother and sister, after putting his father to bed, returned, left their work behind, moved closer together, already sitting cheek to cheek; when now the mother, pointing to Gregor's room, said: "Close the door there, Grete," and when Gregor was in the dark again, while the women next door mixed their tears or even stared tearlessly at the table.

Gregor spent the nights and days almost entirely without sleep. Sometimes he thought that the next time he opened the door he would take charge of the family's affairs just as before; After a long time, the boss and the authorized clerk, the clerks and the apprentices, the house servant who was so insightful, two three friends from other businesses, a maid from a hotel in the provinces, a dear, fleeting memory, a cashier from a hat shop for whom he had seriously but too slowly appeared in his thoughts - they all appeared mixed in with strangers or people who had already been forgotten, but instead of helping him and his family, they were all inaccessible, and he was happy when they disappeared. But then again he was in no mood to worry about his family, only anger at the poor maintenance filled him, and even though he couldn't think of anything he would be hungry for, he made plans how he could get into the pantry so that he could take what was due to him, even if he wasn't hungry. Without thinking any more about how to do Gregor a special favor, the sister hurriedly pushed any food into Gregor's room with her foot before she ran to the shop in the morning and at lunchtime, so that in the evening she could sweep it out with a wave of the broom, regardless of whether the food had perhaps only been tasted or - the most common case - had been completely untouched. Cleaning up the room, which she now always did in the evening, couldn't have been done any quicker. Stripes of dirt ran along the walls, here and there there were clumps of dust and rubbish. At first, when his sister arrived, Gregor positioned himself in such particularly significant angles in order to reproach her, so to speak, with this position. But he could have stayed there for weeks without his sister improving; She saw the dirt just like he did, but she had just decided to leave it alone. With a sensitivity that was completely new to her and that had gripped the entire family, she made sure that tidying up Gregor's room was left to her. Once the mother had given Gregor's room a major cleaning, which she was only able to do after using a few buckets of water - however, all the moisture also hurt Gregor and he lay wide, bitter and immobile on the sofa - but the mother was not left without punishment. The sister had hardly noticed the change in Gregor's room that evening when she, extremely offended, ran into the living room and, despite her mother's raised hands in an imploring manner, burst into a fit of tears, which the parents - the father had of course been startled from his armchair - initially watched in amazement and helplessness; until they too began to stir; the father on the right reproached the mother for not leaving Gregor's room to his sister to clean; On the left, however, the sister screamed at her that she would never be allowed to clean Gregor's room again; while the mother tried to drag the father, who no longer knew himself because of his excitement, into the bedroom; the sister, wracked with sobs, worked the table with her little fists; and Gregor hissed loudly in anger because no one thought to close the door and spare him this sight and noise.

But even if the sister, exhausted from her professional work, had grown tired of caring for Gregor as she had done before, the mother would not have had to stand up for her and Gregor would not have had to be neglected. Because now the operator was there. This old widow, who may have survived the worst in her long life with the help of her strong bones, had no real disgust for Gregor. Without being in any way curious, she happened to open the door to Gregor's room and stopped in amazement at the sight of Gregor, who, completely surprised and despite the fact that no one was chasing him, began to walk back and forth, his hands folded in his lap. Since then, she never failed to open the door a little in the morning and evening and look in at Gregor. At first she also called him over, using words that she probably thought were friendly, such as "Come over here, old dung beetle!" or "Look at the old dung beetle!" Gregor didn't respond to such speeches, but remained motionless in his place, as if the door had never been opened. If only this servant had been given the order to clean his room every day instead of letting her uselessly disturb him according to her whim! Once early in the morning - a heavy rain, perhaps a sign of the coming spring, hit the windows - when the waitress started talking again, Gregor was so angry that he turned against her, as if to attack, albeit slowly and frailly. But the waitress, instead of being afraid, simply lifted up a chair that was near the door, and as she stood there with her mouth wide open, her intention was clear not to close her mouth until the chair in her hand crashed down on Gregor's back. "So we can't go any further?" she asked when Gregor turned around again and calmly put the chair back in the corner.

Gregor now ate almost nothing at all. Only when he happened to pass by the prepared food would he play by putting a bite into his mouth, holding it there for hours and then usually spitting it out again. At first he thought it was his sadness at the state of his room that kept him from eating, but he soon reconciled himself to the changes in the room. People had gotten into the habit of putting things in this room that couldn't be stored elsewhere, and there were now many of these things since one room in the apartment had been rented to three carpenters. These serious gentlemen - all three had full beards, as Gregor once noticed through a crack in the door - were meticulous about maintaining order, not only in their room but, since they had rented a room here, in the entire household, especially in the kitchen. They couldn't stand useless or even dirty stuff. In addition, most of them had brought their own furnishings with them. For this reason, many things had become superfluous that were not for sale but that people did not want to throw away either. All of them went into Gregor's room. Likewise the ash box and the garbage box from the kitchen. The waitress, who was always in a hurry, simply threw whatever was useless at the moment into Gregor's room; Fortunately, Gregor usually only saw the object in question and the hand that held it. The waitress may have had the intention to retrieve the things when the time and opportunity came, or to throw them all out at once, but in reality they remained where they had come with the first throw, unless Gregor wriggled through the junk and got it moving, at first forced because there was no other place to crawl, but later with increasing pleasure, although after such hikes, tired and sad to death, he did not move for hours.

Since the carpenters sometimes had their dinner at home in the common living room, the living room door remained closed on some evenings, but Gregor easily refrained from opening the door, as he had already not taken advantage of many evenings when it was open and had instead lain in the darkest corner of his room without the family noticing. Once, however, the servant had left the door to the living room slightly open, and it remained open even when the carpenters came in in the evening and the light was turned on. They sat down at the table where father, mother and Gregor had previously sat, unfolded the napkins and picked up a knife and fork. Immediately her mother appeared at the door with a bowl of meat and just behind her her sister with a bowl of piled potatoes. The food was steaming with heavy smoke. The carpenters bent over the bowls placed in front of them as if they wanted to examine them before eating, and in fact the one sitting in the middle, who seemed to be an authority to the other two, cut up a piece of meat that was still on the bowl, apparently to determine whether it was tender enough and whether it should not be sent back to the kitchen. He was satisfied, and his mother and sister, who had been watching intently, began to smile with relief.

The family itself ate in the kitchen. Nevertheless, before going into the kitchen, the father came into this room and, with a single bow, cap in hand, walked around the table. The carpenters all stood up and murmured something into their beards. When they were alone, they ate in almost complete silence. It seemed strange to Gregor that one could always hear their chewing teeth amid all the various sounds of eating, as if this was supposed to show Gregor that you need teeth to eat and that even with the most beautiful toothless jaws you can't do anything. “I have an appetite,” said Gregor worriedly, “but not for these things. How these carpenters feed themselves, and I perish!”

Just that evening - Gregor didn't remember hearing the violin the entire time - it sounded from the kitchen. The carpenters had already finished their supper, the middle one had pulled out a newspaper, given a sheet to each of the other two, and now they leaned back and read and smoked. When the violin began to play, they became attentive, stood up and tiptoed to the anteroom door, where they stood huddled together. They must have heard them from the kitchen, because the father called out: “Perhaps the gentlemen are uncomfortable with this game? It can be adjusted immediately." "On the contrary," said the middle gentleman, "wouldn't the young lady like to come in and play here in the room, where it is much more comfortable and cozy?" "Oh please," cried the father, as if he were the violin player. The gentlemen went back into the room and waited. Soon the father came with the music stand, the mother with the music and the sister with the violin. The sister calmly prepared everything for the game; the parents, who had never rented rooms before and therefore exaggerated their politeness towards the landlords, did not even dare to sit on their own armchairs; the father was leaning against the door, his right hand stuck between two buttons of his closed livery coat; But the mother was offered a chair by a gentleman and, leaving the chair where the gentleman had accidentally placed it, sat apart in a corner.

The sister began to play; Father and mother, each from his side, carefully followed the movements of her hands. Gregor, attracted by the game, had ventured a little further and his head was already in the living room. He was hardly surprised that he had shown so little consideration for others lately; Previously, this consideration had been his pride. And he would have had more reason to hide right now, because because of the dust that was everywhere in his room and flew around at the slightest movement, he too was completely covered in dust; He carried threads, hair, and leftover food around on his back and sides; His indifference to everything was far too great for him to lie on his back and rub the carpet, as he had done several times during the day. And despite this situation, he was not afraid to move forward a little on the immaculate living room floor.

However, no one paid attention to him either. The family was completely occupied with playing the violin; The carpenters, on the other hand, who had initially positioned themselves, with their hands in their trouser pockets, far too close behind the sister's music stand so that they could all have seen the music, which must have disturbed the sister, soon withdrew to the window, with their heads bowed, while chatting in hushed tones, where they remained, watched with concern by their father. It really seemed as if they were disappointed in their expectation that they would hear a beautiful or entertaining violin performance, were fed up with the whole performance and were only allowing their peace to be disturbed out of politeness. In particular, the way they all blew smoke from their cigars out of their noses and mouths suggested that they were very nervous. And yet the sister played so beautifully. Her face was tilted to the side, her eyes following the lines of music, searching and sad. Gregor crawled forward a little more and kept his head close to the ground so that he could possibly meet their eyes. Was he an animal because music moved him so much? He felt as if the path to the unknown food he longed for was being shown to him. He was determined to get to his sister, tug on her skirt and thereby indicate to her that she should come into his room with her violin, because no one here was worth playing the game as he wanted it to be worth it. He didn't want to let her out of his room anymore, at least not as long as he lived; his frightening figure was to become useful to him for the first time; He wanted to be at all the doors of his room at the same time and hiss at the attackers; The sister, however, should not stay with him under compulsion, but rather voluntarily; She was supposed to sit next to him on the sofa, leaning her ear towards him, and he would then confide to her that he had had the firm intention of sending her to the conservatory and that, if misfortune hadn't intervened, he would have done so last Christmas - surely Christmas was already over? -- would have told everyone without bothering about any objections. After this explanation, the sister would burst into tears of emotion, and Gregor would rise to her armpit and kiss her neck, which she had worn freely without a ribbon or collar since she went to the shop.

"Mr. Samsa!" the middle gentleman called out to his father and, without saying another word, pointed his index finger at Gregor, who was slowly moving forward. The violin fell silent, the middle carpenter first smiled at his friends, shaking his head, and then looked back at Gregor. The father seemed to think it was more necessary, instead of driving Gregor away, to calm down the carpenters, even though they weren't at all upset and Gregor seemed to entertain them more than playing the violin. He rushed to them and tried to push them into their room with his arms outstretched and at the same time use his body to block their view of Gregor. They actually got a little angry now; it was no longer clear whether it was because of their father's behavior or because of the realization that they had now realized, without knowing it, that they had a roommate like Gregor. They demanded explanations from their father, raised their arms, tugged restlessly at their beards and only slowly backed away towards their room. In the meantime, the sister had overcome the forlorn state into which she had fallen after the suddenly stopped playing, and after holding the violin and bow in her casually hanging hands for a while and continuing to look at the music as if she were still playing, she suddenly pulled herself together, placed the instrument on her mother's lap, who was still sitting in her armchair with breathing difficulties and her lungs working violently, and ran into the next room, to which the carpenters, under the urging of the Father was already approaching faster. You could see how the blankets and cushions in the beds flew up and arranged themselves under the nurse's practiced hands. Before the gentlemen had even reached the room, she had finished putting herself in bed and slipped out. The father seemed to be so caught up in his stubbornness again that he forgot all the respect he owed his tenants. He just pushed and pushed until the middle gentleman stamped his foot thunderously in the doorway of the room, causing his father to stop. "I hereby declare," he said, raising his hand and looking at his mother and sister, "that in view of the disgusting conditions prevailing in this apartment and family" - at this he suddenly spat on the floor - "I am giving up my room immediately. Of course, I won't pay anything for the days that I lived here, but I will still think about whether I will make any - believe me - very easily justified demands against you." He was silent and looked straight ahead of him, as if he was expecting something. In fact, his two friends immediately joined in with the words: "We are also quitting immediately." He then grabbed the door handle and closed the door with a bang.

The father staggered to his chair with groping hands and let himself fall into it; It looked as if he was stretching out for his usual evening nap, but the strong nodding of his head, as if unsteady, showed that he was not at all asleep. Gregor had been lying quietly the whole time on the spot where the carpenters had caught him. The disappointment at the failure of his plan, or perhaps also the weakness caused by so much starvation, made it impossible for him to move. He feared with a certain certainty that a general collapse would be unleashed upon him in the next moment and waited. He wasn't even startled by the violin, which fell from her mother's lap from under her trembling fingers and made a resounding sound.

“Dear parents,” said the sister, slamming her hand on the table as an introduction, “things can’t go on like this. If you don't see that, I see it. I don't want to say my brother's name in front of this monster, so I just say: we have to try to get rid of it. We tried everything humanly possible to look after it and tolerate it, I don't think anyone can blame us in the slightest."
"She's right a thousand times over," said the father to himself. The mother, who still couldn't find enough breath, began to cough dully into her hand with an insane look in her eyes.

The sister rushed to her mother and held her forehead. The father seemed to have been given more definite ideas by his sister's words; he sat upright, played with his servant's hat between the plates that were still on the table from the carpenters' supper, and occasionally looked at the silent Gregor.

“We have to try to get rid of it,” the sister now said exclusively to the father, because the mother couldn’t hear anything in her coughing, “it’ll kill you both, I can see it coming. If you have to work as hard as we all do, you can't endure this constant torture at home. I can't do it anymore either." And she burst into tears so violently that her tears flowed down onto her mother's face, from which she wiped them with mechanical movements of her hands.
"Child," said the father with compassion and striking understanding, "but what should we do?"
The sister only shrugged her shoulders, a sign of the perplexity that had now gripped her as she cried, in contrast to her earlier sense of security.
"If only he understood us," said the father, half questioning; While weeping, the sister shook her hand violently as a sign that this was out of the question.
“If he understood us,” repeated the father, closing his eyes and taking in his sister’s conviction that this was impossible, “then perhaps an agreement with him would be possible. But like this--"

“It has to go,” cried the sister, “that’s the only way, father. You just have to try to get rid of the idea that it's Gregor. The fact that we believed it for so long is our real misfortune. But how can it be Gregor? If it were Gregor, he would have long since realized that it is not possible for people to live together with such an animal and would have left voluntarily. We would then have no brother, but we could live on and honor his memory. But as it is, this animal is chasing us, driving away the landlords, apparently wanting to take over the entire apartment and make us spend the night in the street. "Look, father," she suddenly cried out, "he's starting again!" And in a terror that was completely incomprehensible to Gregor, the sister even left her mother, literally pushed herself off her chair, as if she would rather sacrifice her mother than stay near Gregor, and rushed behind her father, who, only excited by her behavior, also stood up and half raised his arms in front of her as if to protect his sister.

But it never occurred to Gregor to want to scare anyone, especially his sister. He had only started to turn around to go back to his room, and this was certainly noticeable because, due to his suffering condition, he had to help with the difficult turns with his head, which he raised and banged against the floor many times. He paused and looked around. His good intention seemed to have been recognized; it had only been a momentary terror. Now everyone looked at him in silence and sadness. The mother lay in her armchair, her legs stretched out and pressed together, her eyes almost closed with exhaustion; The father and sister were sitting next to each other, the sister had her hand around her father's neck.

“Now maybe I can turn around,” thought Gregor and began his work again. He couldn't suppress the panting of exertion and had to rest now and then. Besides, no one pressured him; everything was left to him. When he completed the turn, he immediately began to walk straight back. He was amazed at the great distance that separated him from his room and did not understand how, given his weakness, he had recently traveled the same path almost without noticing it. Always intent on crawling quickly, he hardly paid any attention to the fact that no word or exclamation from his family disturbed him. Only when he was already in the door did he turn his head, not completely, because he felt his neck stiffen, but he could still see that nothing had changed behind him, only his sister had gotten up. His last look was at his mother, who was now completely asleep.

As soon as he was inside his room, the door was quickly pushed shut, bolted and locked. Gregor was so startled by the sudden noise behind him that his legs buckled. It was the sister who had rushed. She had already stood there upright and waited, then she jumped forward lightly, Gregor hadn't even heard her coming, and she shouted "Finally!" to her parents while she turned the key in the lock.

“And now?” Gregor asked himself and looked around in the dark. He soon discovered that he could no longer move at all. He wasn't surprised by this; rather, it seemed unnatural to him that he had actually been able to move around with these thin little legs until now. Otherwise he felt relatively comfortable. He had pains all over his body, but it seemed to him that they were gradually getting weaker and weaker and would eventually go away completely. He barely felt the rotten apple in his back and the inflamed surroundings, which were completely covered in soft dust. He thought back on his family with emotion and love. His opinion that he had to disappear was perhaps even more decided than his sister's. He remained in this state of empty and peaceful reflection until the tower clock struck the third hour of the morning. He saw the beginning of the general lightening outside the window. Then, without his will, his head sank completely, and his last breath issued feebly from his nostrils.

When the servant came early in the morning - out of sheer strength and haste, she slammed all the doors, no matter how often she had been asked not to, so that a peaceful sleep was no longer possible in the entire apartment from the moment she arrived - she initially found nothing special in her usual short visit to Gregor. She thought he was deliberately lying there so motionless, pretending to be offended; she gave him credit for all sorts of sense. Because she happened to be holding the long broom in her hand, she tried to use it to tickle Gregor from the door. When there was no success there either, she became angry and pushed into Gregor a little, and only when she had pushed him out of his place without any resistance did she become aware. When she soon realized the true situation, her eyes widened, she whistled to herself, but she didn't stay there for long, instead she tore open the bedroom door and called out into the darkness in a loud voice: "Just look, it's dead; There it lies, completely dead!”

The Samsa couple sat upright in the marital bed and had to get over their shock about the waitress before they could take her message into account. But then Mr. and Mrs. Samsa, each on his side, quickly got out of bed, Mr. Samsa threw the blanket over his shoulders, Mrs. Samsa came out in only her nightgown; So they entered Gregor's room. In the meantime the door to the living room, where Grete had been sleeping since the landlords moved in, had also opened; She was fully dressed as if she hadn't slept at all, and her pale face seemed to prove that. “Dead?” said Mrs. Samsa and looked up at the waitress questioningly, even though she could check everything herself and even recognize it without checking. "That's what I mean," said the waitress, pushing Gregor's body a long way sideways with the broom to prove it. Mrs. Samsa made a movement as if she wanted to hold back the broom, but she didn't. "Well," said Mr. Samsa, "now we can thank God." He crossed himself, and the three women followed his example. Grete, who didn't take her eyes off the corpse, said: "Look how thin he was. He hasn't eaten anything in such a long time. Just as the food came in, it came out again." In fact, Gregor's body was completely flat and dry; this was only apparent now that he was no longer lifted from his legs and nothing else distracted the view.

"Come in with us for a while, Grete," said Mrs. Samsa with a wistful smile, and Grete went into the bedroom behind her parents, not without looking back at the corpse. The waitress closed the door and fully opened the window. Despite the early morning, the fresh air was already a bit warm. It was already the end of March.

The three landlords came out of their room and looked around in surprise at their breakfast; they had been forgotten. "Where's breakfast?" the middle gentleman asked the waitress sullenly. But she put her finger to her mouth and then hastily and silently waved to the gentlemen to come into Gregor's room. They came too and stood with their hands in the pockets of their slightly worn skirts, around Gregor's body in the now very bright room.

Then the bedroom door opened and Mr. Samsa appeared in his livery, with his wife on one arm and his daughter on the other. Everyone was a little teary; Grete sometimes pressed her face against her father's arm.

"Leave my apartment immediately!" said Mr. Samsa and pointed to the door without letting the women go. “What do you mean?” said the middle gentleman, somewhat dismayed, and smiled sweetly. The other two held their hands behind their backs and rubbed them together constantly, as if in anticipation of a big argument, which had to turn out in their favor. “I mean it exactly as I say it,” answered Mr. Samsa, walking in line with his two companions towards the master carpenter. At first he stood there quietly and looked at the floor, as if things were putting themselves together in a new order in his head. "Then let's go," he said and looked up at Mr. Samsa, as if, with a sudden humility that came over him, he was demanding new approval even for this decision. Mr. Samsa just nodded at him briefly several times with wide eyes. The gentleman then actually took long strides into the anteroom; His two friends had been listening for a while with very steady hands and were now practically hopping after him, as if in fear that Mr. Samsa would enter the anteroom before them and disrupt the connection with their guide. In the anteroom, all three took their hats from the clothes rack, pulled their sticks out of the cane container, bowed silently and left the apartment. With what turned out to be a completely unfounded mistrust, Mr. Samsa came out onto the forecourt with the two women; Leaning against the railing, they watched as the three gentlemen slowly but steadily descended the long staircase, disappearing into a certain bend in the stairwell on each floor and emerging again after a few moments; The deeper they got, the more the Samsa family lost interest in them, and when a butcher's journeyman with a stretcher on his head rose proudly towards them and then high above them, Mr. Samsa soon left the railing with the women and everyone returned to their apartment as if relieved.

They decided to spend today resting and walking; Not only did they deserve this break from work, they absolutely needed it. And so they sat down at the table and wrote three letters of apology, Mr. Samsa to his management, Ms. Samsa to her client, and Grete to her principal. While I was writing, the servant came in to say that she was going away because her morning work was finished. The three writers at first just nodded without looking up, only when the waitress still didn't want to leave did they look up angrily. “Well?” asked Mr. Samsa. The waitress stood in the doorway smiling, as if she had great luck to report to the family, but would only do so if she was questioned thoroughly. The almost upright little ostrich feather on her hat, which had annoyed Mr. Samsa throughout her entire service, swayed slightly in all directions. “So what do you actually want?” asked Mrs. Samsa, who the waitress still had the most respect for. “Yes,” answered the waitress, unable to continue straight away because of her friendly laughter, “so you don’t have to worry about how the stuff next door is going to be removed. It's okay." Mrs. Samsa and Grete bent down to their letters as if they wanted to continue writing; Mr. Samsa, who noticed that the waitress was about to begin describing everything in detail, resolutely blocked this with an outstretched hand. But since she wasn't allowed to tell the story, she remembered the great hurry she was in, shouted, apparently offended: "Adjes everyone," turned around wildly and left the apartment with the door slamming terribly.

"She will be released in the evening," said Mr. Samsa, but received neither an answer from his wife nor his daughter, because the waitress seemed to have disturbed the calm she had barely regained. They got up, went to the window and stayed there, holding each other. Mr. Samsa turned around in his chair and watched them quietly for a while. Then he called out: “Come here then. Finally leave the old things behind. And also show a little consideration for me." The women immediately followed him, rushed to him, caressed him and quickly finished their letters.

Then all three left the apartment together, something they hadn't done for months, and took the electric car outside the city. The car in which they sat alone was bathed in warm sunshine. Leaning back comfortably in their seats, they discussed the prospects for the future, and upon closer inspection they found that they were not at all bad, because all three positions, which they had not actually asked each other about yet, were extremely favorable and particularly promising for later. The greatest immediate improvement in the situation would of course come easily from a change of residence; They now wanted to take a smaller and cheaper, but better located and generally more practical apartment than the current one that Gregor had chosen. While they were talking like this, Mr. and Mrs. Samsa, looking at their increasingly lively daughter, almost simultaneously remembered how she had recently blossomed into a beautiful and voluptuous girl, despite all the care that had made her cheeks pale. Becoming quieter and communicating almost unconsciously through looks, they thought that it was now time to look for a good man for them. And it was like a confirmation of their new dreams and good intentions when, at the destination of their journey, their daughter was the first to rise and stretch her young body.
